transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Let's get started on the courtyard set design review for Soundstage 3. As you all know, we're weighing two options: a masonry courtyard set or a modular painted-timber courtyard set. Our approved construction budget is $180,000, and fabrication can't begin until we've completed this review and I've signed off on the final construction plan. I'd like to hear from each of your departments — structural, permits, stunt, and insurance — so we can evaluate both options before I make my decision. Who'd like to start?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I need to share my structural findings before we go further. Yesterday's load test showed that the masonry courtyard set would exceed Soundstage 3's 600 kilograms-per-square-meter floor limit. The modular painted-timber design does pass, but only if we install a 30-millimeter load-spreading deck. My written report is still working through the engineering queue, so I wanted to make sure everyone had this information now.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: I need to share what I confirmed with the local heritage-permit office this morning. The approved facade may be no wider than exactly 8 meters, and on-stage masonry cutting is prohibited. I should note that the permit clerk's email has not yet been added to the production file, but these constraints are confirmed and will affect which design option is viable — particularly the masonry option, given the cutting prohibition.

transcript.text: I need to share my rehearsal assessment before we go further. The scripted horse dismount requires an unobstructed lane exactly 10 meters long and 4 meters wide, with a 2-meter crash mat at its landing end. This is a hard requirement for whichever design we choose — the lane needs to be clear of any obstructions, columns, or set dressing along its full length and width. The choreography note is still awaiting the next stunt meeting, but I wanted everyone to have this information now so it can factor into the design decision.

transcript.text: I need to share my insurance findings before we go further. I confirmed with the insurer's underwriter that our coverage excludes any open-flame brazier on this stage. However, an LED-flame prop is permitted under the policy, but only if it remains at least 12 meters from the sprinkler-head cluster and its certification is filed before filming begins. The endorsement for this is currently awaiting countersignature, but these constraints are confirmed and should factor into the design decision — particularly if the courtyard set calls for any fire or flame elements.
